reviewNotes: No person has reviewed this file.

Crux is 10.2, not 10.3. 10.2 is where a percentage is defined as a rate per 100 (IM goal 1 and the second learning target), IM’s narrative says the last two questions “should be the focus of the activity”, and the cool-down (8 dimes, a set of coins worth 130%) asks the same kind of question. 10.3 carries goal 2, the double number line; a reviewer could argue for it, but it applies the definition 10.2 gives.

Testable object: the 6 quarters sentence, each pair’s answer to the last question with its reason. IM’s Clarify, Critique, Correct support tests it directly: before pairs share it, the class fixes a flawed explanation that calls 6 quarters “50% of the value of a dollar.”

IM’s own moments used: the “no dollars in one cent” misconception (10.1), the cents-equals-percent pattern (10.2), the share-successful-strategies synthesis (10.2), the fractions-on-the-ticks misconception (10.3), and the Clarify, Critique, Correct run and breakdown (from IM’s support and the routine catalog).

Premo’s moments: “It’s 150” with no % or “of a dollar” (the language moment; IM’s synthesis calls a percentage with no % symbol incomplete), “6 dimes is 6%” (counting coins, not value; IM names this for the cool-down’s 8 dimes, in the Teacher Guide only), and “Diego’s coins are worth $150” in 10.3.

Two rehearsed moments upstream of the crux are not possible: only the warm-up comes before 10.2. One upstream moment is the warm-up’s “no dollars in one cent”; the other five rehearsed moments are at the crux.

The share order in m4 (cents first, then quarter by quarter, then a quarter is 25% so 6 quarters is 6 × 25%) is Premo’s. IM says to select successful strategies and, if no one reasons with ratios, to illustrate it; it gives no order.

IM’s 10.3 English-learner support (Compare and Connect) was not split out by the extractor: IM spells its tag line “Design Principles(s):”, so the support and its tag stay in 10.3’s synthesis lines. It doesn’t affect the crux.
Student responses and the cool-down were transcribed from the Teacher Guide page images by a model, not checked by a person.

cruxWhy: 10.2 is where students learn that a percentage is a rate per 100, which is IM’s first goal for the lesson. IM says the last two questions, 6 dimes and 6 quarters, “should be the focus of the activity.” The cool-down asks the same kind of question with 8 dimes. IM’s language support, Clarify, Critique, Correct (MLR 3), sits in 10.2’s closing discussion.

object.name: the 6 quarters sentence
object.what: Each pair’s answer to the last question, what percentage of a dollar the value of 6 quarters is, with its reason. Before pairs share it, the class fixes a flawed explanation that says 50%.

goal: Students explain that a percentage is a rate per 100, and name coin amounts as a percentage of a dollar, including amounts over 100%.
rigorCheck: Does every pair still write the 6 quarters sentence with the % symbol, and fix the flawed explanation before sharing it?

watchFor.10.1: A student says there are no dollars in one cent.
watchFor.10.2: “6 quarters is 150” with no % symbol, or “50%” from 150 − 100.
watchFor.10.3: Top ticks labeled \(\frac{1}{4}\), \(\frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{3}{4}\) instead of dollar values.

moments.see: On the last question, a student says: “Zero. There are no dollars in one cent.”
moments.means: They know a cent is much less than a dollar. The question asks what part of a dollar one cent is.
moments.say: What fraction of a dollar is one cent?
moments.evidence: In response to “how many dollars are in one cent,” students might say there are no dollars at all in one cent. Ask them what fraction of a dollar one cent represents.
criteria: Asked what part of a dollar one cent is
Took “no dollars” as a starting point, not a wrong answer

moments.see: For the dimes question, a student writes “6%.”
moments.means: They counted coins, not cents. The percentage is about the value of the coins, per 100 cents.
moments.say: How many cents are 6 dimes worth?
moments.dont: Write 60 cents next to it for them.

moments.see: A student says: “It’s easy. The percentage is just the number of cents.”
moments.means: True here, because a dollar is 100 cents. It only works when 100% is 100 of something, which is why IM ends the activity on a double number line.
moments.say: That works for a dollar. Why does it work?
moments.dont: Call the shortcut wrong, or let it pass as a rule.
moments.evidence: Students may notice a pattern particular to this activity—that the percent value is the same as that for cents—and carry that assumption forward and apply it incorrectly to situations in which 100% does not correspond to 100.
criteria: Agreed the pattern works for a dollar
Asked why, so the 100 cents came from them
Didn’t let it stand as a rule for every percentage

moments.see: Pairs have answers for 6 dimes and 6 quarters. Before anyone shares the last one, you uncover the flawed explanation.
moments.means: Clarify, Critique, Correct (MLR 3) gives students someone else’s flawed writing to fix. This one subtracts 100 cents from 150 and calls it 50% of a dollar. IM says to listen for pairs who clarify the wording: 50% greater than a dollar, or 150% of a dollar.
moments.say: Here’s someone’s explanation of 6 quarters. What’s wrong with it?

runSheet.step: Before pairs share the 6 quarters answer, show the flawed explanation.
Pairs find the error and critique the reasoning.
Listen for pairs who clarify the wording: “50% greater than a dollar,” or “150% of a dollar.”
A few pairs read theirs aloud, then the class shares strategies.

moments.dont: Skip the flawed explanation and go straight to pairs’ answers.
moments.evidence: Ask students to identify the error, critique the reasoning, and write a correct explanation.
criteria: Showed the flawed explanation before pairs shared their own
Had pairs find the error and write a correct explanation
Listened for pairs who clarified the wording

moments.see: Pairs read “50% of the value of a dollar,” then look up at you. You start rewriting it on the board.
moments.means: The flawed explanation is there for students to improve. If you fix it, they only copy.
moments.say: What would you change? Fix it with your partner first.
moments.dont: Correct the explanation for the class.
moments.evidence: for students to improve upon the written work by correcting errors and clarifying meaning.
criteria: Handed the flawed explanation back to the pairs
Gave partners time to fix it together first
Didn’t rewrite the explanation for the class

moments.see: Fixing the flawed explanation, a student says: “It’s 150. Not 50. 150.”
moments.means: The number is right. The % symbol and “of a dollar” are missing, and IM counts a percentage with no % symbol as an incomplete answer.

emerging.say: 150 what? Of what? Point and show me.
emerging.move: They point to the 6 quarters, then to the dollar bar, and say or write the percentage with its symbol. They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.
emerging.nonverbal: They draw a 100-cent bar for the dollar, then a longer bar for 6 quarters, and write the % on it.

developing.say: 150 what? Of what? Use your frame.
developing.move: With the frame, they tell a partner what 6 quarters are worth in cents and what percentage of a dollar that is. They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.

expanding.say: 150 what? Of what? Then say what the explanation meant.
expanding.move: They say the percentage with its symbol, then reword the flawed line so it’s true: “50% greater than a dollar.” They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.

moments.dont: Say “150% of a dollar” for them.
criteria: Asked every level the same question: what the 150 is, and of what
Matched the way in to the student’s level
Didn’t say the percentage sentence for them

moments.see: On desks for 6 quarters: cents (“150 cents, so 150%”), quarter by quarter, and one coin’s percentage (“6 × 25%”).
moments.means: IM says to share successful strategies and make sure someone reasons with ratios, a quarter is 25% so 6 quarters is 6 times that. One order that works: cents first, ratio reasoning last.
moments.say: Start us off. How did you get 6 quarters?
moments.evidence: Select students with successful strategies to share their thinking with the class.
criteria: Ended on ratio reasoning: one coin’s percentage, times the number of coins
Didn’t share only the cents shortcut

moments.see: A student labels the top ticks \(\frac{1}{4}\), \(\frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{3}{4}\).
moments.means: The fractions are right. The question asks for dollars, so the ticks work better as dollar values.
moments.say: Those are right. What is each one in dollars?
moments.evidence: Consider prompting them to write fractional values as cents or to rewrite the cents as dollar values.

moments.see: For the 150% question, a student writes “$150.”
moments.means: They carried over the cents pattern from 10.2. Here 100% lines up with 1 dollar, not 100.
moments.say: Find 100% on the line. What is it worth?

patterns.says: “There are no dollars in one cent.”
patterns.why: They read “how many dollars” as whole dollars.
patterns.shows: They know a cent is far less than a dollar. Part of a dollar is next.
patterns.evidence: students might say there are no dollars at all in one cent.

patterns.shows: They know a percentage compares with a whole. Value per 100 cents is next.

patterns.why: Every answer so far has matched the number of cents.
patterns.shows: They see the pattern. Why it works, 100 cents in a dollar, is next.
patterns.evidence: Many students may reason by noticing a pattern—that the number of cents in an amount matches its percentage of a dollar (e.g., 60 cents is 60%)—rather by thinking in terms of ratio or scaling.

patterns.why: They scale one coin’s percentage, the ratio reasoning IM wants early.
patterns.shows: Percentage as a rate they can scale, like a unit rate.
patterns.evidence: a student may think that if a dime is 10% of a dollar, then 6 dimes is 60% of a dollar.

patterns.says: “6 quarters is 50%, because it’s 50 cents more than a dollar.”
patterns.why: They found the difference, then named it as a percentage of a dollar.
patterns.shows: They compared with a dollar. Saying what the 50 is “more than” is next.
patterns.evidence: the author probably meant to say that 6 quarters is 50% greater than the value of a dollar

patterns.why: The number is clear to them; the % and “of a dollar” feel extra.
patterns.shows: They found the value of 6 quarters as a percentage of a dollar.

patterns.says: “A dollar and two dimes is 120%, and so is four quarters and four nickels.”
patterns.why: They build an amount over 100% from different coins.
patterns.shows: Percentages above 100%, the case IM says students rarely meet.
patterns.evidence: Answers vary. Sample response: A dollar and two dimes, four quarters and four nickels

patterns.why: Earlier number lines from 0 to 1 used fractions.
patterns.shows: They split 0 to 1 into four equal parts. Dollar values are next.
patterns.evidence: students may label the tick marks with fractions instead of the decimal value of the coins.

predict.context: Pairs fill in the cents for six U.S. coins and match each to a percentage of a dollar. Then they answer two questions: what percentage of a dollar the value of 6 dimes is, and the value of 6 quarters.
predict.question: What will most pairs write for the 6 quarters sentence?
predict.countQuestion: How many pairs will write 150% with the % symbol and a reason?
predict.countUnit: pairs will write 150% with the % symbol and a reason.
predict.tell: If few do, “of a dollar” and the % symbol aren’t part of their answer yet. The flawed explanation is where they fix that: the third moment you’ll rehearse.

emerging.entry: On the third read, they point to each coin in the picture in order, then to the 25-cent and 100-cent bars.
emerging.frame: The value of ___ is ___ cents. A dollar is 100 cents. So it is ___% of a dollar.
emerging.does: They can say what each coin is worth in cents.
emerging.reaching: Writing a percentage with its % symbol, and saying it is “of a dollar.”
emerging.stretch: They say the whole sentence aloud, with “of a dollar.”

developing.entry: On the third read, they say one way to start: find the cents, or use one coin’s percentage. They tell their partner what is wrong with “50%,” then write a correct line together with the frame. They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.
developing.frame: The value of ___ is ___ cents, and a dollar is 100 cents. A percentage is a rate per 100, so it is ___% of a dollar. It is more (or less) than 100% because ___.
developing.does: They can find the cents in a group of coins and say a number for the percentage.
developing.reaching: Saying the percentage as a rate per 100: “150 cents per 100 cents.”
developing.stretch: They check it another way: one coin’s percentage of a dollar, times the number of coins.

expanding.entry: On the third read, they name two ways to start and say which they would use. They rewrite the flawed explanation so it is true, read it to another pair, and make it clearer once. They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.
expanding.frame: One ___ is ___% of a dollar, so ___ of them is ___% of a dollar. Another way: ___.
expanding.does: They can explain the 6 quarters answer with cents and the % symbol.
expanding.reaching: Saying what the flawed line meant: 50% greater than a dollar, not 50% of a dollar.
expanding.stretch: They say why a percentage can be more than 100%.

cuts.note: Keep it short: one or two students per question, then move on.
Leave out the 120% extension unless pairs finish early. Move quickly through the first two questions; IM says the last two are the focus. Share two pairs, not three.
Don’t cut it: it carries IM’s second goal, the double number line, and the lesson synthesis uses it. If short of time, take Elena’s question as a class.

neverCut: Quiet think time before partners talk in 10.2
The 6 quarters sentence, with the % symbol
Fixing the flawed “50%” explanation before pairs share
IM’s closing double number line: 100 cents lined up with 100%

inClass.launch: “A rate per 1 was a unit rate. What might a rate per 100 mean?”
sequence: A pair who found the cents, then compared with 100 cents
A pair who went quarter by quarter past 100%
A pair who used one coin’s percentage times the number of coins

beforeClass: Write IM’s flawed explanation on chart paper and keep it covered until pairs have answered 6 quarters.
Have IM’s closing double number line ready to draw: 0, 50, 100, 150 cents above 0%, 50%, 100%, 150%.
